# Optimal Control of Stochastic Cauchy Evolution Problems with Non-Standard Boundary Dynamics

This paper investigates the optimal control problem for a class of stochastic Cauchy evolution problems characterized by non-standard boundary dynamics and control. The study addresses a challenging setting in which the control acts not only on the interior of the system but also through its boundary behavior, giving rise to a rich and intricate mathematical structure.

The model under consideration couples an infinite dimensional dynamical system with a finite dimensional dynamics. This coupling reflects the interplay between two distinct components of the system: the primary evolution, which takes place in an infinite dimensional state space, and an auxiliary process, which is governed by a finite dimensional description. The interaction between these two components lies at the heart of the problem and constitutes the main source of both its theoretical interest and its analytical difficulty.

More precisely, the finite dimensional dynamics describes the boundary conditions of the internal system. Rather than being prescribed in a static or predetermined manner, the behavior at the boundary evolves according to its own dynamical law. In this way, the boundary itself becomes an active element of the model, carrying its own state and contributing to the overall evolution of the coupled system.

What renders these boundary conditions non-standard is that the value at the boundary is governed by a separate stochastic differential equation. Consequently, the boundary does not merely impose a constraint on the interior evolution; instead, it possesses an independent stochastic dynamics that interacts with the infinite dimensional component. This formulation departs significantly from classical boundary value problems, in which the boundary data are either fixed or determined directly by the internal state, and it necessitates the development of appropriate analytical and control-theoretic tools to address the resulting coupled stochastic system.

# Optimal Control of Stochastic Cauchy Evolution Problems with Dynamic Boundary Conditions

## Introduction

The study of optimal control problems for stochastic evolution equations has become an increasingly important area of research, bridging the gap between infinite-dimensional analysis, stochastic calculus, and control theory. In this paper, we investigate the optimal control problem for a class of stochastic Cauchy evolution problems that exhibit non-standard boundary dynamics. Unlike classical formulations, where boundary conditions are either fixed or prescribed in a static manner, our framework considers boundary values that themselves evolve according to their own stochastic dynamics.

## Problem Formulation

The central innovation of our approach lies in the coupling of two distinct dynamical systems. On one hand, we have an infinite-dimensional dynamical system that governs the evolution of the state within the interior of the domain. This system is typically described by a stochastic partial differential equation formulated in an appropriate Hilbert or Banach space setting. On the other hand, we introduce a finite-dimensional dynamics that governs the behavior of the boundary conditions, which is described by a separate stochastic differential equation.

This coupling reflects physical and engineering scenarios in which the boundary of a system is not merely a passive constraint but rather an active component with its own evolutionary law. The boundary value, in this setting, does not remain fixed nor follow a predetermined trajectory; instead, it responds dynamically to both its own intrinsic stochastic forcing and its interaction with the interior state. This creates a genuinely coupled system in which the interior dynamics influence the boundary evolution and, reciprocally, the boundary dynamics feed back into the interior evolution.

## Significance of the Approach

The proposed framework addresses a significant gap in the existing literature by providing a rigorous mathematical treatment of these unconventional boundary conditions. Traditional approaches to stochastic evolution equations typically assume homogeneous boundary conditions or treat inhomogeneous boundary data as external inputs. In contrast, our formulation recognizes that in many realistic applications—ranging from fluid dynamics with moving interfaces, to thermal systems with reactive boundaries, to control problems in structural mechanics—the boundary itself must be modeled as a dynamic entity subject to random perturbations.

By coupling an infinite-dimensional interior dynamics with a finite-dimensional boundary dynamics, we obtain a mathematical structure that is both flexible enough to capture a wide range of applications and tractable enough to permit rigorous analysis. The finite-dimensional nature of the boundary dynamics is particularly noteworthy, as it corresponds to situations where the boundary behavior can be effectively parameterized by a finite number of degrees of freedom, while the interior retains the full complexity of an infinite-dimensional system.

## Contributions and Outlook

Our work provides a significant approach for handling coupled systems with dynamically controlled boundaries. Within this framework, we establish the well-posedness of the underlying coupled stochastic system and formulate the associated optimal control problem. The control objective seeks to minimize a suitable cost functional that accounts for both the interior state and the boundary dynamics over a specified time horizon, subject to the coupled stochastic evolution constraints.

The results developed herein open new avenues for the analysis and application of stochastic control theory to systems with active boundaries. They lay the groundwork for further investigations into the derivation of optimality conditions, the characterization of optimal controls, and the development of numerical methods suited to this class of problems. Ultimately, this framework contributes to a deeper understanding of controlled stochastic systems in which the interplay between interior and boundary dynamics plays a fundamental role.

## The Cauchy Distribution

The Cauchy distribution is a fascinating and unusual probability distribution that holds an important place in mathematics and statistics. Named after the French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy (1789–1857), it is notable for its distinctive properties that set it apart from more common distributions like the normal distribution.

### Key Characteristics

The Cauchy distribution is defined by its bell-shaped curve, which superficially resembles the normal distribution. However, the similarities end there. The most remarkable feature of the Cauchy distribution is that it has **no defined mean, variance, or higher moments**. This counterintuitive property makes it a favorite example in statistics courses to illustrate the limitations of certain mathematical assumptions.

### Mathematical Definition

The probability density function of the standard Cauchy distribution is given by:

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1 + x^2)}$$

The distribution can be generalized with a location parameter (x₀) and a scale parameter (γ), allowing it to be shifted and stretched to fit various applications.

### Real-World Applications

Despite its unusual nature, the Cauchy distribution appears in several practical contexts:

- **Physics**: It describes the resonance behavior in spectroscopy and is known as the Lorentz distribution in that field.
- **Signal Processing**: The distribution models certain types of noise and interference.
- **Finance**: It is sometimes used to model extreme events and heavy-tailed phenomena.

### Why It Matters

The Cauchy distribution serves as a crucial reminder that not all distributions behave "nicely." Its heavy tails mean that extreme values occur more frequently than one might expect, making it valuable for understanding phenomena where outliers play a significant role.

In summary, the Cauchy distribution stands as an elegant example of how mathematical objects can defy our intuitions while still providing meaningful insights into the natural world.

# Abstract

This paper investigates optimal control problems governed by stochastic evolution equations subject to dynamic boundary conditions. We consider a class of semilinear stochastic partial differential equations driven by cylindrical Wiener processes, where the boundary dynamics are described by an additional evolution equation coupled to the interior system. Such formulations arise naturally in models of heat conduction with thermal memory at the boundary, diffusion processes with reactive surfaces, and various physical phenomena where boundary effects evolve dynamically in time under random perturbations.

We first establish the well-posedness of the state equation within an appropriate functional-analytic framework, formulating the problem as an abstract stochastic evolution equation on a product Hilbert space that simultaneously accounts for the bulk and boundary components. Under suitable Lipschitz and growth conditions on the nonlinear terms, existence and uniqueness of mild solutions are proven, together with continuous dependence on the control and initial data.

The central contribution concerns the derivation of necessary optimality conditions in the form of a stochastic maximum principle. By introducing the adjoint backward stochastic evolution equation associated with the coupled system, we characterize optimal controls through a variational inequality involving the Hamiltonian. Particular attention is devoted to the interplay between the interior and boundary adjoint variables, which reflects the nontrivial coupling structure inherent in dynamic boundary conditions. Under convexity assumptions, we further show that these conditions are sufficient for optimality.

Finally, we discuss the associated Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation via the dynamic programming approach and illustrate the theoretical results with applications to stochastic reaction–diffusion systems. Our findings extend classical optimal control theory to a broad class of stochastic systems with active boundary dynamics and provide a foundation for further numerical and computational investigation.

# Stochastic Cauchy Problems with Dynamic Boundary Conditions Driven by Coupled SDEs

## 1. Introduction

The classical abstract Cauchy problem, in which the evolution of a state in a Banach space $X$ is governed by a generator $A$ subject to a fixed or deterministically evolving boundary constraint, has long provided a unifying framework for the study of partial differential equations of parabolic and hyperbolic type. In this paper we consider a substantially more general setting in which the boundary datum is itself a stochastic process, evolving according to its own stochastic differential equation and coupled to the interior dynamics through the boundary operator.

More precisely, let $(A, D(A))$ be a densely defined closed operator on a separable Hilbert space $H$, and let $L : D(L) \to \partial H$ denote a surjective boundary operator onto an auxiliary boundary space $\partial H$. We study the coupled system
$$
\begin{cases}
\, du(t) = A u(t)\, dt + F\big(u(t), \xi(t)\big)\, dW(t), & t > 0, \\
\, L u(t) = \xi(t), & t \geq 0, \\
\, d\xi(t) = b\big(\xi(t)\big)\, dt + \sigma\big(\xi(t), u(t)\big)\, dB(t), & t \geq 0,
\end{cases}
$$
where $W$ and $B$ are (possibly correlated) cylindrical Wiener processes, and the boundary process $\xi$ takes values in $\partial H$. The essential novelty lies in the third equation: rather than prescribing the trace $Lu$ as a given function of time, we allow it to fluctuate randomly, with drift $b$ and diffusion $\sigma$ that may depend on the interior state $u$.

Such problems arise naturally in the modeling of physical systems subject to random forcing at an interface—for instance, heat conduction in a body whose surface temperature is maintained by a noisy thermostat, or fluid flow through a domain with a randomly fluctuating inflow condition. The mathematical difficulty stems from the interplay between the unboundedness of $A$, the fact that the boundary condition is inhomogeneous and time-dependent, and the feedback loop by which the interior state influences the very boundary process that constrains it.

Our approach rests on a reformulation of the boundary value problem via the Dirichlet operator and the associated abstract framework of Greiner, which allows us to recast the coupled system as a stochastic evolution equation on the product space $H \times \partial H$. We then establish existence and uniqueness of mild solutions under suitable Lipschitz and growth hypotheses on $F$, $b$, and $\sigma$, and we investigate the regularity of the resulting solution map together with the long-time behavior of the coupled process.

# Control Problem: PDE-SDE Coupled System with Stochastic Boundary Dynamics

Here's a formulation of a control problem combining infinite-dimensional PDE dynamics with finite-dimensional stochastic boundary dynamics.

## Physical Motivation

Consider a **flexible thermal/mechanical structure** (e.g., a heat conductor, elastic beam, or acoustic domain) whose boundary is attached to a **finite-dimensional mechanism** (actuator, sensor, or rigid body) subject to random disturbances. This models scenarios like:

- A heated rod with a thermally-actuated valve at its endpoint experiencing noisy load
- A flexible beam coupled to a rigid mass with stochastic external forcing
- A fluid domain with a mechanical boundary actuator under random perturbations

## Mathematical Formulation

### Interior PDE Dynamics (Infinite-Dimensional)

Let $u(x,t)$ evolve on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with boundary $\partial\Omega = \Gamma_c \cup \Gamma_0$. A typical example is a heat/diffusion equation:

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x,t) = \nabla \cdot (a(x)\nabla u) + f(x,t), \quad x \in \Omega, \ t > 0
$$

with a Dirichlet condition on the uncontrolled part:

$$
u(x,t) = 0, \quad x \in \Gamma_0
$$

### Boundary SDE Dynamics (Finite-Dimensional, Stochastic)

On the controlled boundary $\Gamma_c$, the boundary value is *not* prescribed directly but is governed by a **stochastic differential equation** for a state $\xi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^m$:

$$
d\xi(t) = \big[ A\,\xi(t) + B\, v(t) + G\, \mathcal{T}u(t) \big]\,dt + \Sigma\, dW(t)
$$

where:
- $\xi(t)$ — finite-dimensional boundary mechanism state
- $v(t)$ — **control input** (your actuation)
- $W(t)$ — $k$-dimensional Wiener process (stochastic disturbance)
- $\Sigma$ — noise intensity matrix
- $\mathcal{T}u(t)$ — a **trace/flux operator** coupling the PDE back to the boundary, e.g. the normal flux $\mathcal{T}u = -a\,\partial_\nu u|_{\Gamma_c}$

### Coupling Condition

The two systems are coupled through the boundary condition linking $u$ on $\Gamma_c$ to $\xi$:

$$
u(x,t) = C\,\xi(t), \quad x \in \Gamma_c
$$

This makes $\xi$ act as a **dynamic boundary condition** — the boundary value evolves according to its own stochastic dynamics, driven partly by the PDE's flux and partly by control and noise.

## Abstract State-Space Form

Writing the combined state as $z(t) = \big(u(\cdot,t),\, \xi(t)\big) \in \mathcal{H} = L^2(\Omega) \times \mathbb{R}^m$, the system takes the form of a **stochastic evolution equation**:

$$
dz(t) = \big[\mathcal{A}\, z(t) + \mathcal{B}\, v(t)\big]\,dt + \mathcal{G}\,dW(t)
$$

where $\mathcal{A}$ is an (unbounded) operator on the product space $\mathcal{H}$ encoding both the diffusion generator and the boundary SDE drift, with domain $D(\mathcal{A})$ enforcing the trace compatibility $u|_{\Gamma_c} = C\xi$.

## Control Objective

A natural **stochastic optimal control problem** minimizes an expected cost:

$$
J(v) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T \Big( \|u(\cdot,t) - u_d\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 + |\xi(t)|_Q^2 + |v(t)|_R^2 \Big)\,dt + \Phi(z(T)) \right]
$$

subject to the coupled dynamics, seeking a feedback law $v(t) = \mathcal{K}\,z(t)$ (or an output-feedback version if only partial noisy measurements are available).

---

## Key Challenges to Highlight

1. **Unbounded boundary coupling** — the trace/flux operators are unbounded, requiring careful functional-analytic setup (analytic semigroups, admissibility conditions).
2. **Well-posedness** — establishing existence of mild/variational solutions for the stochastic PDE with dynamic boundary conditions.
3. **Infinite-dimensional Riccati equations** — the LQG/optimal feedback requires solving operator Riccati equations on $\mathcal{H}$.
4. **Noise regularity** — boundary noise can be spatially rough, raising questions about the regularity of $u$.

---

Would you like me to:
- Specify a **concrete example** (e.g., 1D heat equation with a spring-mass boundary)?
- Develop the **optimal control / Riccati** theory in detail?
- Focus on **well-posedness and semigroup** framework?
- Adapt this to a **wave/beam equation** instead of diffusion?

# Introduction

The optimal control of systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a mature and richly developed area of applied mathematics, with foundational contributions dating back to the seminal work of Lions [cite]. When such systems are subjected to random perturbations—arising from environmental noise, model uncertainty, or intrinsic fluctuations—the appropriate mathematical framework becomes that of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs). The corresponding optimal control theory has attracted sustained attention over the past several decades, motivated both by its intrinsic analytical challenges and by a broad spectrum of applications ranging from mathematical finance and population dynamics to the control of turbulent flows and the management of distributed physical processes.

A substantial portion of the existing literature on stochastic control of SPDEs is devoted to systems in which control acts distributively throughout the spatial domain, or in which noise and control enter through classical boundary conditions of Dirichlet, Neumann, or Robin type. In many physically relevant situations, however, the mechanism of control is not distributed across the domain but is instead confined to its boundary, and moreover the boundary itself may evolve according to its own dynamics. Such **dynamically controlled boundary conditions**—in which the boundary data are governed by an auxiliary evolution equation that is itself subject to control and, potentially, to stochastic forcing—fall outside the scope of the standard theory. Problems of this nature arise naturally in the modeling of heat exchange through active surfaces, the regulation of chemical concentrations across permeable membranes, thermoacoustic systems, and a variety of fluid–structure interaction phenomena, where the interface between the system and its environment carries nontrivial dynamics of its own.

The presence of non-standard, dynamically controlled boundary conditions introduces several difficulties that are absent in the classical setting. First, the coupling between the interior SPDE and the boundary evolution equation gives rise to a system whose natural state space is a product of function spaces of differing regularity, complicating both the formulation of well-posedness and the derivation of the requisite a priori estimates. Second, the low spatial regularity typically associated with boundary noise, together with the unbounded nature of the operators mediating the boundary coupling, renders the standard variational and semigroup techniques inapplicable without significant modification. Third, the control enters the dynamics in a manner that is neither purely distributed nor of standard boundary type, which necessitates a careful reformulation of the associated optimality conditions and adjoint calculus.

In this paper we address the optimal control of a class of stochastic partial differential equations equipped with such dynamically controlled boundary conditions. Our objectives are threefold. We first establish the well-posedness of the controlled state system, proving existence, uniqueness, and appropriate regularity of solutions within a suitably chosen functional-analytic framework that accommodates the coupled interior–boundary dynamics. We then formulate the associated optimal control problem for a general convex cost functional and prove the existence of an optimal control. Finally, we derive first-order necessary optimality conditions in the form of a stochastic maximum principle, characterizing the optimal control through an appropriately defined adjoint system—a backward stochastic partial differential equation coupled, in turn, to a backward boundary equation reflecting the structure of the forward dynamics.

The principal contributions of this work may be summarized as follows. We introduce a rigorous mathematical formulation for a class of SPDEs with dynamically controlled boundary conditions that has not, to our knowledge, been treated in full generality in the existing literature. We develop the analytical tools required to handle the coupling between interior and boundary dynamics under stochastic forcing, and we establish a complete optimality theory for the resulting control problem. In doing so, we extend the reach of stochastic PDE control theory to a setting of considerable practical relevance while clarifying the structural role played by the boundary dynamics in the optimality system.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the notation, the functional-analytic setting, and the standing assumptions, and presents the precise formulation of the state equation and the control problem. Section 3 is devoted to the well-posedness and regularity theory for the controlled state system. Section 4 establishes the existence of optimal controls and derives the necessary optimality conditions via the stochastic maximum principle. Section 5 discusses illustrative examples and the applicability of the abstract results, and Section 6 concludes with remarks on possible extensions and directions for future research.
